headline: The 2026 update keeps Shimer's job-finding story (β_F≈0.89 in normal times) but adds one rare 'layoff regime' — active only 0.2% of months (March–April 2020) — where separations drive 81% of the unemployment surge; meanwhile the flows have slowed (ω: 0.47→0.34), making unemployment 53% more persistent.

figures.caption: A: separation share of each postwar recession's unemployment surge — 2020 (0.81, orange) is the lone regime above the constant-β model's ~0.16 band; 2008 (0.17) confirms the original story out of sample. B: the flows have slowed secularly (ω=F̄+X̄, blue) so unemployment-deviation persistence ρ=1−ω (orange) has risen, lengthening the half-life 1.08→1.66 months.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left: bar chart of separation share by recession, all near a dashed 0.16 line except a tall orange 2020 bar at 0.81. Right: blue line of adjustment speed falling from ~0.55 to ~0.34 over 1950–2026 with a dashed orange persistence line rising.

notes: Reuses follow-up 001's constructed FRED series (vintage 2026-08-24); no re-fetching or re-running the original pipeline. Original comparison values read from 001 CSVs / the paper text (cited in report.md).

Compute-modest per instruction: regime probabilities are frequencies and β's are the paper's OLS decomposition on regime subsamples/windows — calibration to moments 001 produced, not a likelihood-based Markov-switching estimation.

β_F^L's magnitude is calibrated to 2020-inclusive windows, not predicted out-of-sample: 2020 is the only extreme layoff on record, so its size is unpredictable from history — itself the tail-risk finding. The OOS-validated part is the regime classifier (flags exactly Mar–Apr 2020).

2020 is sub-quarterly; analysis is monthly and the clipped March-2020 F point is handled with a clip-immune separation hypothetical (with the clip kept, recent steady-state corr spuriously collapses to 0.24).
